full_caption: Quarrytown Holdings, LLC, Appellant, v. Cordelia Brackenbury, Appellee
court: Westmarch District Court of Appeal, Second District
fictional_notice: FICTIONAL DOCUMENT. Generated for the LegalCase Responder demo corpus. The parties, court, docket number and holdings below are invented and do not correspond to any real case, court, or person.

sections.heading: Paragraph 1
sections.text: Quarrytown Holdings, LLC and Cordelia Brackenbury own riparian tracts along the Mill Race Creek within Rooksbury County. The dispute concerns Cordelia Brackenbury's diversion of approximately 1,050 gallons per minute for irrigation of 8.9 acres.

sections.heading: Paragraph 2
sections.text: A prescriptive water right may be acquired by open, adverse diversion for the statutory period, but only as against a use that was actually interfered with during that period.

sections.heading: Paragraph 3
sections.text: Severed mineral rights carry an implied easement to use so much of the surface as is reasonably necessary to extract the minerals, but that right is qualified by an obligation to accommodate existing surface uses where reasonable alternatives exist.

sections.heading: Paragraph 4
sections.text: A use that wholly deprives a downstream riparian of water for domestic purposes is unreasonable as a matter of law, without regard to the economic value of the upstream use.

sections.heading: Paragraph 5
sections.text: Reasonableness is a question of fact informed by the purpose of the use, its economic and social value, the extent of the harm, the practicality of avoiding the harm, and the protection of existing investments.

sections.heading: Paragraph 6
sections.text: Accretion belongs to the riparian owner; avulsion does not change the boundary. The 2000 channel shift, being sudden and perceptible, was avulsive and left the boundary at the former thread of the stream.

sections.heading: Paragraph 7
sections.text: Under the riparian doctrine as modified in this State, each riparian owner is entitled to a reasonable use of the watercourse, measured against the correlative rights of other riparians.

sections.heading: Paragraph 8
sections.text: Groundwater in this State is governed by the rule of reasonable use, under which an overlying owner may withdraw for beneficial use on the overlying land but may not export off-tract to the injury of neighboring wells.

sections.heading: Paragraph 9
sections.text: The 77 days of well failure experienced by Quarrytown Holdings, LLC coincided with the operation of Cordelia Brackenbury's high-capacity irrigation well 30 feet from the shared aquifer boundary. Causation was established by drawdown modeling.

sections.heading: Paragraph 10
sections.text: The accommodation doctrine required Cordelia Brackenbury to consider directional drilling from an off-site pad before siting the wellpad within the irrigated circle. Failure even to evaluate the alternative defeats the claim of reasonable necessity.

sections.heading: Paragraph 11
sections.text: The injunction is modified to permit diversion not exceeding 200 gallons per minute between April and July, and is otherwise affirmed.

sections.heading: RIDER E — BOUNDARY, ACCRETION AND PUBLIC TRUST
sections.text: Where the boundary is a watercourse, gradual accretion and reliction move the boundary with the water; a sudden and perceptible avulsive change does not, and the boundary remains at the former thread of the stream. Nothing in this instrument conveys any interest in the bed of a navigable water, title to which is held by the State in trust for the public.

sections.heading: Clause 1 — Attorney's Fees
sections.text: In any action to enforce or construe this instrument, the prevailing party shall recover its reasonable attorney's fees, expert fees and costs, at trial and on appeal. Where the instrument grants fees to one party only, this clause shall be read as reciprocal and shall entitle the other party to fees on the same terms if that party prevails.

sections.heading: Clause 2 — Notice
sections.text: Every notice required or permitted shall be in writing and shall be deemed given: on personal delivery; on the third business day after deposit in the United States mail, certified, return receipt requested, postage prepaid; or on the next business day after deposit with a nationally recognized overnight courier. Notices to a party shall be sent to the address last furnished by that party in writing. Electronic mail alone does not constitute notice unless the recipient acknowledges receipt in writing.
